title: Case: commercetools, Shopware and the Composable Movement
basis: Reconstructed from the published chapter (posts/49-case-composable-movement/index.md) and its former spec.md, whose Non-goals, Modalities, Open questions, Decision log, Sources and Changelog are carried over. One spec paragraph per unit of the chapter, plus the units the contract asks for and the published chapter did not have: a thesis paragraph and a roadmap in the introduction, a chapter synthesis that answers the opening, Part XI's closing (synthesis across chapters 46 to 49, so-what, callback to the part opening) and the journal's closing (Eva's five promises, the toolkit, the hand-off to the appendix tutorial). These are recorded in decision_log.

know: The 2020 promise: the MACH Alliance founded in June 2020 by commercetools, Contentstack, EPAM and Valtech around Microservices, API-first, Cloud-native and Headless; over 100 members by December 2023; what the promise did not say (who builds and runs the storefront, who owns the joins and what they cost each year, for which size of merchant the difference pays).

commercetools' dated turn: a new CEO in July 2024; about 10% of staff cut in February 2025 after missed 'aggressive revenue growth targets'; AgenticLift (January 2026) 'on top of your existing commerce solution'; 'Autonomous Commerce' (June 2026); Core Commerce and Product Catalog sold as standalone modules 'without replacing their existing platforms' (July 2026); a Gartner Leader for the seventh year (October 2026); the April and July 2026 figures not reconciled by the vendor; the reasons for the turn only the chapter's labeled inference.

The other paths: Shopware (first among the 1,000 largest German B2C shops in EHI's 2026 study at 12.5%, GMV-based plans with a paid plan required above €1 million of GMV, Nexus and Shopware Payments on PayPal's infrastructure from June 2026, PayPal holding more than 40%); Adobe Commerce's three deployment options and Commerce Optimizer beside any backend; the Mage-OS fork; BigCommerce renamed Commerce.com in July 2025 and reporting in August 2026 that B2C replatforming 'remains softer than historically'.

The alliance's principles from four letters (2020, restated 2023) to five principles including Incremental (August 2025) to three, Open, Composable and Connected (November 2026), with microservices and headless gone; its February 2026 survey of 600 decision-makers, with 37% naming integration complexity a primary concern; the cost lines of an assembly (storefront, joins, upgrades, separate services, licenses, people, exit) and the conditions under which it fits.

Where the evidence stops: no vendor reason for the turn, no published method behind Shopware's integration-cost claims, no independent study comparing the total cost of an assembly with a hosted platform plus layers.
believe: Composable was right about properties (open APIs, replaceable capabilities, clear ownership) and wrong about prescriptions (rebuild as services, build your own storefront).
Open source and composable are independent choices: choose on who owns upgrades and joins, not on the license.
can_do: Cost a composable proposal including the storefront, every join, upgrades on the vendors' schedules, people and exit.
Decide whether a missing capability should be adopted as one service beside the current platform, and name its owner.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a composable replatforming proposal for a merchant with an integration-shaped team, the reader states what to ask and what to decide, grounded in the movement's own record.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A consultancy proposes that a brand with about €60 million in revenue, twelve people in technology (mostly integration engineers), a hosted platform and about 30 integrations replace the platform with a composable stack: an API-only engine, a built storefront, search, content and an integration layer. Using only this chapter: what should the brand ask, and what should it decide?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Ask what the 2020 promise did not say: who builds and runs the storefront the engine does not ship and at what yearly cost; who owns each join, its API version and its renewal date; who upgrades everything built against the vendors' services on their schedules; which reference customer is within a factor of ten of the brand's size. The assembly would have more joins than today, all of them the brand's. The movement's own record: its alliance dropped microservices and headless from its principles, its 2026 survey has 37% naming integration complexity a primary concern, and commercetools now sells modules for adoption without replacing existing platforms. A full assembly fits a Group-stage merchant with platform and product teams and a storefront that competes; with an integration-shaped team the brand should keep its platform and adopt the capability it cannot own (an OMS, a PIM, search) as one service beside it with a named owner.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can read a vendor alliance's adoption figures critically and name the finding that runs against its interest.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A vendor deck says: '78% of organizations with fully scaled MACH technology see clear AI ROI, and 85% of technology leaders increased their MACH share.' Using only this chapter: how should a reader treat these figures?
acceptance_criteria.expected: As the alliance's own claims: surveys commissioned by a vendor alliance and answered by a population that includes its adopters, with 'clear ROI' undefined and the 2023 release's applicant totals internally inconsistent, so they do not show that a merchant cut costs or raised sales. Keep each figure's definition, date and unit attached (commercetools' April and July 2026 figures differ and are not reconciled). The usable finding is the one against interest: 37% of respondents name integration complexity a primary concern. Vendor figures such as Shopware's 15 tools, 52% of effort and 40% savings have no published method; no independent study compares the total cost of an assembly with a hosted platform plus layers.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can tell an open-source platform from a composable assembly.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this chapter: is moving to an open-source platform such as Shopware a move to composable commerce?
acceptance_criteria.expected: No; open source and composable are different axes. Shopware's core is open, but its commercial path is to be the hub: plans priced on GMV, a paid plan required above €1 million of GMV, Nexus as an orchestration layer that replaces middleware, and Shopware Payments on PayPal's infrastructure, pulling integration and payments into the platform. commercetools is proprietary and service-shaped. Choose on who owns upgrades and joins, not on the license.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: That a merchant wanting to replace one capability without the others still depends on shared product identifiers, prices and stock updates, so the cost of changing those connections decides whether assembling services pays; MACH as founded in June 2020 (microservices, API-first, cloud-native, headless) and over 100 members by December 2023, with headless as a narrower choice; dated accounts from commercetools, Shopware, Adobe and the alliance, including later services attached to existing platforms; the flagship's turn to layers (the February 2025 cut, AgenticLift, standalone modules in July 2026), Shopware pulling integration and payments into its platform, and the alliance rewriting its principles while its survey names integration complexity; failure patterns The Giant's Boots, The Burned Bridge and The Spaghetti Junction; Eva's order as the thread. Evidence: vendor releases, pricing pages, the alliance's pages and survey, filings and trade press, with inferences labeled.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the draft, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as sections[].paragraphs[].

audience.who: Readers new to commerce architecture who will meet 'composable' in a replatforming pitch, an analyst chart or a conference talk: most of all engineers and product managers deciding whether to adopt a capability as a separate service; second, leaders who must judge a consultancy's composable proposal.
already_knows: What buying something online is like from the shopper's side; roughly what an API, a database and a queue are.

Parts I to X: the thirteen steps of an order, promise and handoff, the three status lines, 'system', 'the shop platform' for the hosted product, the four scale stages (Starting, Growing, Omnichannel, Group), system of record, single writer, events, idempotency and reconciliation; available-to-promise; the failure-pattern names (The Giant's Boots, The Burned Bridge, The Spaghetti Junction among them); agentic commerce from chapter 45.
Glosses already given: PSP, WMS, ERP, iPaaS, EDI, webhook, API call, SKU, channel, marketplace connector, 3PL, order management system (OMS), availability service, D2C, B2B, PIM, POS.

Kestrel & Pine: a fictional outdoor brand with fourteen people in technology on a hosted shop platform, its 34 integrations, its agency, Eva's jacket order of 13 April 2027 and her five promises, the Black Friday 2026 incidents, the February 2027 pitches and the Waypoint decisions W1 to W8.

Part XI's method (dated public sources, documented versus inferred, each case ending where its evidence stops) and chapters 46 to 48: Shopify's kept monolith and its integration contract, Amazon's move to services after a 2001 wall and its cart and seller-of-record split, Zalando's 2015 split, later narrowing and 2025 read API.
does_not_know: Composable commerce, the MACH Alliance and the four words (microservices, API-first, cloud-native, headless); headless as a narrower choice.
GMV and run-rate as vendor metrics; Gartner's Magic Quadrant and Forrester's Wave as analyst placements.
commercetools, Shopware, Adobe Commerce and Commerce Optimizer, Mage-OS, Commerce.com, Saleor as vendors and what each sells.
Fair-usage policy priced on GMV; orchestration layer; platform-as-a-service versus fully managed SaaS.

thesis.question: What did the composable movement promise, what does a full assembly cost a merchant, and what does the movement's own record from 2024 to 2026 show about when assembling commerce from parts is right?
thesis.claim: The composable movement promised replaceable services in 2020 and asked the merchant to build the storefront and own every join between services, work for a product-engineering team before the first sale. By 2026 the MACH Alliance had dropped microservices and headless from its principles, 37% of its 2026 survey named integration complexity a primary concern, and commercetools sold modules for existing platforms. A full assembly fits multi-brand groups with platform teams; merchants without one add one owned service at a time.
thesis.disputed_by: The 2020–2023 pitch that composable is where commerce is going: a merchant should replace its suite or hosted platform with best-of-breed services and a built storefront, because each capability can then be swapped and the merchant escapes a single vendor's release cycle.
thesis.so_what: A merchant that accepts the claim answers a composable proposal by asking which of the four 2020 words (microservices, API-first, cloud-native, headless) and the three 2026 principles (open, composable, connected) the proposer means, who builds and runs the storefront, who owns each join with its API version and renewal date, and whether the missing capability can be adopted as one service beside the current platform. Kestrel & Pine declined the consultancy's February 2027 composable rebuild (a separate engine, storefront, search, content system and integration layer for fourteen technology staff, about €3.2 million over three years, illustrative) and takes the per-capability path as Waypoint: an OMS, availability and a PIM beside the hosted platform, each integration with an owner and a contract, revisited at the 2029 review.
thesis.how_why: Every capability bought as a separate service adds a join, a contract, an API version, a renewal and an owner, and an API-only engine ships no storefront, so the running cost of an assembly falls on the merchant's own team (storefront, integration, upgrades on the vendors' schedules) before the first sale, which a team shaped for integration rather than product engineering cannot carry. The vendors' 2026 products (commercetools' AgenticLift and standalone modules, Adobe Commerce Optimizer beside any backend, Shopware pulling integration and payments into its platform) are sold to merchants who keep their core; no release explains the turn, and its link to commercetools' 2025 cuts is the chapter's labeled inference.

supporting_claims.claim: The 2020 MACH promise (microservices, API-first, cloud-native, headless) described how enterprises with product-engineering teams could build; it did not say who builds and runs the storefront, who owns the joins between services and what they cost each year, or for which size of merchant the difference pays.

commercetools, the movement's flagship, turned between 2024 and 2026 from selling replacement to selling layers and standalone modules for platforms merchants keep, after a February 2025 staff cut tied to missed growth targets; no release gives the reason, so the link is a labeled inference.

The other vendors absorbed the word rather than decomposing: Shopware pulled integration and payments into an open-source platform priced on GMV, Adobe sells composable layers beside any backend, the Magento forks lengthen the patch chain and Commerce.com adopted the vocabulary while reporting weak replatforming, which shows that open source and composable are independent choices.

The alliance's own record states the correction: its principles dropped microservices and headless between 2020 and 2026, and 37% of respondents to its February 2026 survey named integration complexity a primary concern, the cost line the 2020 promise left out.

A full assembly adds the storefront, every join, upgrades on the vendors' schedules, separate contracts, people and exit to the merchant's own bill, so it fits a Group-stage merchant with platform and product teams, while an Omnichannel merchant such as Kestrel & Pine adopts one owned capability at a time beside a kept platform.

The public record stops short of the vendors' reasons and of any independent cost comparison, so the chapter's reasons are labeled inference and its costs are labeled judgment or Kestrel & Pine illustrations.

role.contribution: Tests the book's stay-and-surround recommendation against the vendors that sold the opposite, setting out the assembly's cost lines and the movement's own move to layers beside a kept core, and performs the part's closing followed by the journal's closing on the same page (the published chapter does neither: it ends with one sentence listing the four cases and a hand-off to domain-coverage).

additional_patterns.applies_to: promise to commercetools: the 2020 promise before the 2024-2026 turn
commercetools, shopware and adobe: the flagship's turn to layers set against vendors that absorbed the word
costs to kp: the cost lines, then the conditions under which assembly fits, then the merchant's path

flow.rationale: The 2020 promise and its unsaid column come first, because every later section tests it. The vendors' record follows as evidence: the flagship first (it carried the promise furthest), then the vendors that went the other way or absorbed the word, so the turn is seen from several sides before the alliance's own wording is read. The alliance's principles and survey come after the vendors because they state, in the movement's own words, the correction the vendors' products already show. Only then are the costs and the conditions argued, because they rest on that record; Kestrel & Pine applies them; 'Where the Evidence Stops' closes the body because it bounds every case just read. Putting the costs before the record would state the author's judgment before the evidence; putting the alliance first would read a rewrite whose reason the vendors' turn supplies; moving 'Where the Evidence Stops' up to follow the survey would split the vendors' limits from the cost limits that the cost table and the Kestrel & Pine illustration add.

hook.content: A merchant wants to replace its search service without replacing checkout and the catalog as well; buying separate services seems to offer that freedom, but each still depends on shared product identifiers, prices and stock updates, so replacement is practical only if those connections can be changed at an acceptable cost.

bridge.to_topic: The composable movement sold the services shape to every merchant from June 2020; its vendors' and its alliance's dated record from 2020 to 2026 shows what the promise left out and when assembly pays.

sections.heading: Adobe, the Forks and Commerce.com: Composable as a Deployment Option
sections.controlling_idea: Adobe, the Magento forks and Commerce.com absorbed the composable word as a deployment option, a fork or a rename rather than adopting decomposition.

advances_thesis.how: Adds three more vendors whose record shows the word absorbed, not adopted.

flow.rationale: Three vendors with the same pattern follow one claim: the suite (Adobe), the open-source side it left (the forks) and the SaaS side (Commerce.com). The forks follow Adobe because they are forks of its open-source edition; Commerce.com comes last because its August 2026 report that replatforming is weak sets up the alliance's own rewrite. Putting the forks first would describe a fork of a product not yet introduced.

transition_in.introduces: Three more vendors absorbing the word.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Adobe, the community forks of its open-source edition and Commerce.com show the composable word being absorbed rather than adopted.
Adobe Commerce now lists three deployment options and sells Commerce Optimizer to work alongside any backend, so composable has become a layer a suite vendor sells beside any backend.

evidence.what: On-premises, cloud infrastructure (PaaS), Cloud Service (managed SaaS); Commerce Optimizer 'alongside an existing Adobe Commerce or third-party commerce backend'; partner reports for June 2025 launches.
evidence.shows: Shows a suite selling a layer beside a kept backend.

transition_in.introduces: The suite vendor.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The Mage-OS fork gives a merchant the most freedom in the chapter and the longest patch chain: Adobe, then the distribution, then the agency, then the merchant.

evidence.what: Organized 2021, incorporated 2022; releases 3.6.0 and 4.0.0 in October 2026; no shareholders; 216-plus financial contributors.
evidence.shows: Shows the open-source side and its patch chain.

transition_in.introduces: The community fork of its open-source edition.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: BigCommerce renamed itself Commerce.com in July 2025 with composable vocabulary and kept its engine, and a year later reported flat revenue and B2C replatforming 'softer than historically'.

evidence.what: Rename 31 July 2025; Q2 2026 revenue $84.5 million, up 0.1%; 'remains softer than historically' (SEC exhibit, 6 August 2026).
evidence.shows: Shows a vendor adopting the word while the replatforming market weakened.

transition_in.introduces: The SaaS side.

sections.heading: The Alliance Rewrites Its Principles
sections.controlling_idea: The alliance's own principles went from four words to five principles to three, dropping microservices and headless, the clearest evidence of the turn.

advances_thesis.how: Records the correction in the movement's own words.

transition_in.introduces: The alliance rewriting it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The alliance's stated principles changed from 'Microservices, API-first, Cloud-Native, and Headless' (2020, restated 2023) to five guiding principles, Composable, Connected, Incremental, Open and Autonomous (August 2025), to three, Open, Composable and Connected (November 2026).

evidence.what: Three dated rows quoting each formulation with its source.
evidence.shows: Shows the wording change side by side.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: With microservices and headless gone and 'Incremental' added in 2025, the author's labeled reading is that the acronym outlived its expansion: what survives are properties a merchant can ask of any platform, and what was dropped were prescriptions about how the vendor's own software is built.

evidence.what: Figure 2: an old signboard with two words crossed out beside a new board of three.
evidence.shows: Shows what was dropped and what remained.

transition_in.introduces: What the change means for a merchant.

sections.heading: What the Movement's Own Data Say
sections.controlling_idea: The alliance's own 2026 survey, read as a commissioned survey, yields one finding against interest: 37% of respondents name integration complexity a primary concern.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the cost line the promise left out from the movement's own data.

flow.rationale: The survey's figures come first, then how to read them, then the vendor figures that point the same way with the same caveat and the absence of an independent study. Reading the survey before stating its figures would leave the caveats with nothing to qualify.

transition_in.introduces: Its own survey data.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The alliance's February 2026 report on a survey of 600 enterprise technology decision-makers gives favorable AI figures and also reports that 37% cite integration complexity as a primary concern.

evidence.what: 78% versus 13% clear AI ROI; 98% versus 33% AI at scale; 89% missing standards; 37% integration complexity; 45% privacy and security.
evidence.shows: The survey's findings as stated.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Read as a survey commissioned by a vendor alliance with 'clear ROI' undefined, its usable finding is the one against interest: more than a third of respondents name integration complexity a primary concern, the cost line the 2020 promise left out.

evidence.what: Commissioned; population includes adopters; ROI undefined.
evidence.shows: Explains why only the finding against interest is kept.

transition_in.introduces: How to read them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Shopware's integration figures point the same way with the same caveat, and no independent study with a stated method compares the total cost of an assembly with a hosted platform with layers, so the chapter's costs are judgment or illustration.

evidence.what: More than 15 tools; up to 52% of implementation effort.
evidence.shows: A second vendor figure pointing the same way, with a vendor's reason to count high.

transition_in.introduces: A vendor figure that points the same way, and the missing independent study.

sections.heading: What Composable Actually Costs
sections.controlling_idea: A composable assembly carries the same bill as any platform plus lines the brochure assigns to nobody, all of which fall on the merchant's own team.

advances_thesis.how: Turns the unsaid column into cost lines and shows who pays each.

transition_in.introduces: The author's labeled cost table.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A cost table (the author's synthesis) sets a hosted platform with layers beside a composable assembly line by line, storefront, joins, upgrades, separate services, licenses, people and exit, and names who pays each.

evidence.what: Seven cost lines in two columns with who pays; 34 integrations at Kestrel & Pine; Saleor Cloud 0.8% above $200,000 a month.
evidence.shows: Shows each line the assembly adds to the merchant's bill.

evidence.what: Figure 3: the merchant's own team at the centre owning the storefront and every join.
evidence.shows: Shows who carries the added lines.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Kestrel & Pine received such a proposal, an outside consultancy's composable rebuild of February 2027 at an illustrative three-year cost of about €3.2 million; with three storefront and app engineers of fourteen and a €14,000-a-month agency, a built storefront would need at least those engineers full time plus the agency before any of the 34 integrations were rebuilt, and the assembly would have more joins, all its own.

evidence.what: Ledger: fourteen in technology, three storefront and apps engineers, agency €14,000 a month, 34 integrations; the storefront staffing labeled an illustration.
evidence.shows: Works the storefront line through for one merchant.

transition_in.introduces: The February 2027 composable proposal to Kestrel & Pine, and its storefront line worked through.

sections.heading: When Composable Is Right
sections.controlling_idea: Composable is right under specific conditions, scale stage, differentiation, team shape, vendor count and reason to move, and a full assembly is a Group-stage choice while an Omnichannel merchant takes it one capability at a time.

advances_thesis.how: States the conditions the record and the cost lines support.

transition_in.carries_over: The cost of a full assembly.
transition_in.introduces: The conditions under which it is still right.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The record says composable was oversold to the wrong merchants, not that it is wrong, and a fit table gives the conditions under which it fits or limits.

evidence.what: Five situations: scale stage, differentiation, team shape, vendor count, reason to move.
evidence.shows: Gives conditions, not verdicts.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The per-capability path, keeping the platform and adding a PIM, an OMS, search or an agentic layer as owned services, is what the vendors now sell and what an Omnichannel merchant can absorb; the full assembly is a Group-stage choice.

evidence.what: commercetools' July 2026 modules: 'without replacing their existing platforms'.
evidence.shows: Shows even enterprises adopting it piece by piece.

transition_in.introduces: The path most merchants should take.

sections.heading: What Kestrel & Pine Takes From It
sections.controlling_idea: Kestrel & Pine declined the consultancy's composable rebuild costed above and takes the per-capability path the vendors now sell, as Waypoint.

advances_thesis.how: Applies the fit conditions to the book's merchant.

transition_in.introduces: The book's merchant taking it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Kestrel & Pine declined the proposal: Waypoint keeps the hosted platform (W4) while buying an OMS, availability and a PIM beside it, with the warehouse authoritative for stock and each integration owned under a contract (W5), the selective assembly the vendors now sell, revisited at the 2029 review.

evidence.what: W4 stay and surround; W1 stock ownership; W5 integration standards; 2029 review.
evidence.shows: Shows the per-capability path at an Omnichannel merchant.

evidence.what: Figure 4: the 2020 promise asked the merchant to build the storefront and own every join; the 2026 products from the same vendors attach a layer to a platform the merchant keeps.
evidence.shows: Shows Waypoint's shape as the one the vendors' 2026 products attach to.

sections.heading: Where the Evidence Stops
sections.controlling_idea: The record stops short of commercetools' and Shopware's reasons, Adobe's dates, the alliance's reasons, an independent cost study and some analyst placements.

advances_thesis.how: Marks the limits of every case just read.

transition_in.introduces: What the record could not establish.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Six limits: commercetools' reasons and unreconciled figures, Shopware's strategy and claims, Adobe's launch dates, the alliance's reasons and survey method, the absence of an independent cost study, and missing analyst placements.

conclusion.heading: What to Take Away
conclusion.synthesis: The movement's own record now answers the opening merchant: adopt search as one service beside the kept platform with a named owner for its joins; a full assembly replaces every join at once and pays only for a Group-stage merchant with platform and product teams, which is also what the movement's vendors sell by 2026.
conclusion.so_what: A composable proposal is answered with questions about the storefront, each join's owner, version and renewal, reference customers within a factor of ten and the vendor's own products for kept platforms, before any product is compared; and, as Part XI's closing shows, any large-company example is tested by the discipline it shows and the size at which it was adopted.

callback.to: The hook's merchant that wants to replace its search service without replacing checkout and the catalog.
callback.how: p42 answers it: one service beside the kept platform with an owner for its joins to product identifiers, prices and stock; the full assembly is the Group-stage case.

takeaway.content: Ask the seven questions of any composable proposal; test any large-company example by its dated source, the discipline it shows and the machinery only that company needs; then start with the entity-owner table and the integration inventory from the toolkit for your own landscape.

hand_off.carries_over: Part X's account of agentic commerce and the cases' evidence.
hand_off.introduces: One protocol followed message by message.

transition_in.introduces: What the chapter establishes within them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The opening's merchant can now be answered from the movement's own record: adopt search as one service beside the kept platform, with an owner for its joins to product identifiers, prices and stock; a full assembly replaces every join at once and pays only for a Group-stage merchant, which is what the vendors themselves sell by 2026.

evidence.what: The hook; commercetools' modules; the alliance's principles and survey; the cost and fit tables.
evidence.shows: The chapter's answer, drawn from every section and tied back to the opening.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Established: the 2020 definition and the 2026 principles without microservices or headless; the flagship's layers and modules after its 2025 cut; Shopware's move of integration and payments into a GMV-priced platform; the survey's 37%.

transition_in.introduces: What is documented.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Depends on context: a full assembly fits a Group-stage merchant with product and platform teams; one capability as a separate service fits the Omnichannel stage when it has an owner; open source and composable are independent choices.

transition_in.introduces: What depends on the merchant.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The author's synthesis: the movement was right about properties and wrong about prescriptions, and the 2026 products of commercetools and Adobe, a kept core with layers beside it, are composable as it should have been sold.

transition_in.introduces: The author's view.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Seven questions apply the chapter to a composable proposal: which words the proposer means, who runs the storefront, who owns each join, which capability can be one service beside the platform, which reference customer is near the merchant's size, what the vendor sells for kept platforms, and what stands behind each figure.

transition_in.introduces: The questions to ask of a proposal.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: This chapter closes Part XI, which opened with the Giant's Boots: the four cases look like four architectures, but read for what each company wrote about its joins they give one answer, a contract at each join, one owner per fact and a reconciliation, with the shape around them sized to the company's own load, teams or customers.

evidence.what: Shopify's webhook contract and dated withdrawals; Amazon's always-writeable cart and seller-of-record split; Zalando's 2025 read API and deprecation rules; the composable vendors' modules beside a kept platform.
evidence.shows: The part's synthesis across chapters 46 to 49, with the callback to the part opening.

transition_in.introduces: What the four cases of Part XI have in common.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Any large-company example cited in a design review can therefore be tested before it is copied: find the dated source, mark what it documents and what is inferred, and ask which discipline at a join it shows and at what size the company adopted the shape around it; for Kestrel & Pine each case's answer was a Waypoint decision already made (W1, W4, W5, W8) that changed none of its architecture.

evidence.what: W1 stock ownership, W4 stay and surround, W5 integration standards, W8 agent readiness (ledger).
evidence.shows: Shows the test applied to the book's merchant.

transition_in.introduces: The test for any example, and Kestrel & Pine's answers.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The book asked one question of a jacket order, a wholesale reorder, a peak day, an AI agent and four real companies, and got the same kind of answer each time: name the system that may make the promise and the system that must keep it.

evidence.what: Parts IX to XI: the journeys, the decisions over time and the four cases.
evidence.shows: The journal's synthesis.

transition_in.carries_over: The four companies' answer at their joins.
transition_in.introduces: The same answer across the whole book.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Eva's five promises (this jacket, at this price, in stock, on Thursday, returnable) give the test for the reader's next decision before any product is compared: which promise is this, which system makes it and which system has to keep it; the place to start is the entity-owner table and the integration inventory in the toolkit.

evidence.what: Eva's five promises from the introduction; Tools 2 and 3 of the toolkit.
evidence.shows: The callback to the book's opening and the first course of action.

transition_in.introduces: Eva's five promises as the test, and where to start.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: For readers who want one join in full detail, the appendix takes Part X's account of agentic commerce and the cases' evidence down to one protocol followed message by message, and the reference pages follow it.

transition_in.introduces: The appendix and the reference pages.
